content: Deciduous teeth, also referred to as milk teeth, baby teeth, temporary teeth, or primary teeth, represent the initial set of teeth that develop in humans and many other mammals. These teeth begin forming during the embryonic stage of development and become visible in the mouth, or erupt, during infancy. Typically, deciduous teeth are eventually replaced by permanent teeth. However, in cases where permanent replacements are absent, these teeth can remain functional for many years. The formation of deciduous teeth begins during the embryonic phase of pregnancy, specifically around the sixth week of development, when the dental lamina starts to form. This process initiates at the midline and progresses posteriorly. By the eighth week of embryonic development, there are ten distinct areas on both the upper and lower arches that will later develop into the deciduous dentition. These teeth continue to form until they erupt into the oral cavity. The deciduous dentition consists of a total of 20 teeth, with five teeth per quadrant and ten teeth per arch. The eruption of these teeth begins at approximately six months of age and continues until the child is around 25 to 33 months old. The first teeth to appear in the mouth are the mandibular central incisors, while the last to erupt are the maxillary second molars. The deciduous dentition includes central incisors, lateral incisors, canines, first molars, and second molars, with one of each type present in each quadrant, making a total of four of each tooth type. All of these teeth are eventually replaced by their permanent counterparts, except for the first and second molars, which are replaced by premolars. Deciduous teeth typically remain in place until around the age of six, at which point the permanent teeth begin to emerge, resulting in a mixed dentition phase. The eruption of permanent teeth triggers a process known as root resorption, where the roots of the deciduous teeth are dissolved and absorbed by the developing permanent teeth. This process, called exfoliation, involves the shedding of deciduous teeth and their replacement by permanent teeth. Exfoliation generally occurs between the ages of six and twelve, and by the age of twelve, most individuals have only permanent teeth remaining. Deciduous teeth play a critical role in the development of the oral cavity. Dental researchers and dentists emphasize their importance in guiding the eruption of permanent teeth, as the permanent replacements develop from the same tooth bud as the deciduous teeth. This alignment ensures proper spacing and positioning for the permanent teeth. Additionally, the muscles of the jaw and the formation of the jawbones rely on the presence of primary teeth to maintain the appropriate space for the permanent dentition. The roots of deciduous teeth also provide a pathway for the eruption of permanent teeth. Beyond their structural role, deciduous teeth are essential for a child’s ability to chew food effectively and develop proper speech patterns. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry recommends that infants visit a dentist by six months of age or shortly after the eruption of the first primary tooth, and no later than the age of one. During this visit, parents can learn how to care for their child’s deciduous teeth and prevent oral diseases. To minimize the risk of oral disease in deciduous teeth, parents are advised to use orthodontic pacifiers with flattened nipples instead of rounded ones. These pacifiers should not be cleaned in the parent’s mouth to avoid transferring Streptococcus mutans bacteria, which can cause cavities, to the child. Additionally, parents should avoid giving sweet liquids in bottles or sippy cups, as these can lead to tooth decay. Only water or milk should be used in these containers, except during mealtimes. Bottles should not be taken to bed with children, as this practice can result in baby bottle caries, a condition caused by sweet liquids pooling around the teeth while the child sleeps. Dental researchers recommend initiating oral hygiene care as soon as the first tooth erupts, typically around six months of age. Parents can use an infant toothbrush and water for cleaning. Once the child reaches the age of two, a small amount of fluoride toothpaste can be introduced to further protect the teeth.
